title: Lecture 1: Introduction to Deep Learning
text:
Lecturer: Bartek Wilczyński
The first part of this lecture introduced some key concepts in Machine Learning. As I’ve already taken a course in it during my MSc, I didn’t take any notes. However, the lecturer recommended the book “An Introduction to Statistical Learning” which is the same book I used to prepare myself for my ML exam: it is a wonderful book that explains all key concepts in a very simple and clear way and, very importantly, available online for free.
The second part of the lecture gave a summary of the story of Neural Networks. It is interesting but, again, I didn’t take notes. Please refer to the lecture materials.


In the third part of the lecture, we dived into how modern NN models are built and trained. I have learnt that any network consisting of at least three layers (i.e. 2 stacked layers of perceptrons) can be considered “deep” neural networks.

Now, let’s pretend we have a neural network with three layers: there are inputs \(x\), then an hidden layer with a weight \(w_{1}\) and a bias \(b_{1}\). The final layer is the output, this one has also a weight \(w_{2}\) and a bias \(b_{2}\). Training the neural network happens in 3 steps:

Inizializing: weights are usually inizialized randomly, while biases are usually set as 0 or very small numbers.
Forward pass:

inputs (\[x_{i}\]) enter the input layer and then are multiplied for a certain weight (\[w_{i,1}\]) when entering the first layer of “neurons”. Each neuron receives all inputs, each multiplied for a different weight which is specific not only for the input provided, but for the neuron that received them too;
after all inputs, multiplied for their weights, reach a neuron, they are summed with each other and also by a certain amount of bias, specific of the neuron (\(b_{1}\)). We will call the sum of all the weighted inputs and biases for the first neuron \(z_{1}\):
\[z_{1} = w_{i,1}x_{i} + w_{j,1}x{j}+...+b_{1}\]
Before passing the value \(z_{1}\) it down, the neuron needs to be “activated”. That means that, if this value \(z_{1}\), transformed into \(a_{1}\) using a certain “activation function”, doesn’t reach a certain threshold, then the neuron remains inactive and the new input is not passed down.

Activation functions: there are different activation functions, but the most used is the ReLU. We will see why.
\[sigmoid: \space \sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}} \quad \quad tanh: \space tahn(x) \quad \quad ReLU: \space max(0,x)\]

We can pretend, in this example, that the activation function is the sigmoid. \(z_{1}\) is transformed into \(a_{1} = \frac{1}{1+e^{-z_{1}}}\). If \(a_{1}\) reaches a certain threshold, the input passes to the second layer of neurons (in this case, also the output layer). We do the same thing again: we first sum the inputs \(z_{2} = w_{i,2}a_{i} + w_{j,2}a{j}+...+b_{2}\), then we transform the output \(a_{2} = \frac{1}{1+e^{-z_{2}}}\) and, if this reaches the set treshold, it will be out final output (prediction).

Backpropagation:

Now we want to assess the performance of the model. During training, if the result \(a_{2}\) obtained is wrong, we need to correct the weights. How is “wrong” defined? Like in logistic regression, the error is calculated as a Log-Loss function. It is calculated at the very last layer (outputs), by comparing the predicted result (\(a_{2}\)) with the real output we were expecting (\(y\)):
\[LogLoss = -\[y \log(a_{2}) + (1-y)log(1-a_{2})\]\]
Remember, we usually want to optimize a model, which means to minimize a Loss function. In simple terms? We want the Log-Loss to be as close to 0 as possible!
We first calculate the partial derivate of the error (Log-loss) with respect to the weighted sum (\(z_{2}\)), the one that allowed us to calculate the output \(a_{2}\). Because we used the sygmoid (very easy to derivate), the formula can be simplified:
\[\frac{\delta LogLoss}{\delta {z_{2}}} = a_{2} - y\]
Following the chain rule, the impact that the weight had on the error when we calculated \(z_{2}\) is calculated as:
\[\frac{\delta LogLoss}{w_{2}} = \frac{\delta LogLoss}{\delta {z_{2}}} \cdot \frac{\delta z_{2}}{\delta w_{2}}\]
Because \(z_{2} = w_{2} \cdot a_{1}\) the formula can be simplified to \(\frac{\delta Log-loss}{w_{2}} = (a_{2} - y) \cdot a_{2}\).
The weights are updated using the learning rate (\(\eta\)):
\[w_{2, new} = w_{2, old} - \eta \cdot \frac{\delta \text{LogLoss}}{\delta w_{2}}\]
The chain rule allows the error to go back even to the first layer, to correct \(w_{1}\) too:
\[\frac{LogLoss}{w_{1}} = \frac{LogLoss}{z_{2}} \cdot \frac{z_2}{a_1} \cdot \frac{a_1}{z_1} \cdot \frac{z_1}{w_1}\]

What about biases?: they are updated in the same manner!



These steps are repeated many times, in what we call a learning loop. The simples method is to take the lopp over all observations (an epoch) and adapt the weight accordin to the gradient function with a learning rate. If we do this in random order in each epoch, this is a variant of Stochastic Gradient Descent. Usually many learning epochs are needed to reach convergence.



The problem is that some weights have similar gradients while others are oscillating, and it can make it hard to reach the minimum, caused by two main problems:

the gradient can be “pulled” by some weights in the opposite direction than the global minimum (towards a local minimum “preferred” by one of the gradients);
by having only one learning rate, we could be either go too fast or too slow, because some gradients might need a bigger or smaller step than others.

The momentum algorithm adds a rescaled gradient from the previous step to the current gradient, so learning can be faster when gradients are consistent and slower if we start oscillating.
ADAM (ADAptive Momentum estimation) adds another idea: by looking at the first and second moments of the gradient, and adding “forgetting” factors \(\beta_1\) and \(\beta_2\) to the estimation process:

First, it computes the first moment: \(m_t = \beta_1 \cdot m_{t-1} + (1-\beta_1) \cdot g_t\);
then it computes the second moment: \(v_t = \beta_2 \cdot v_{t-1} + (1-\beta_2) \cdot g_t^2\);
both are applied to the weights update: \(w_{new} = w_{old} - \frac{\eta}{\sqrt{v_t}+\epsilon}\cdot m_t\).




Deep learning is prone to overfitting: you could use techniques that are used in standard ML (Lasso and Ridge), but the most popular regularization techniques are based on randomized removal of subsets of weights during training. In case of dilution, during each training epoch a random subset of weights is not updated. In the case of dropout, all weights associated to a subset of neurons will not be used at all. These techniques slow don the process of training but they make the model better.
And, for today, we have finished! See you on the practical part.







As a refresher, the Log-Loss is a function that allows us to maximilize the Likelihood of the data. Said like this, it can sound confusing, but it is not that complicated. Let’s just say that, the probability to observe the true output \(y\), given the computed/predicted output \(\hat{y}\) is:
\[ P(y|\hat{y}) = \hat{y}^{y} \cdot (1-\hat{y})^{(1-y)}\]
This is simply a Bernoulli distribution (the output is either 1 or 0). But we don’t have only one input nor neuron (which would mean only one weight to optimize), but a whole set, and we want to maximize the probability of observing the “true output” for the entire dataset, not only one neuron. When we talk about Maximum Likelihood, we mean that we want to maximize how close our neural network can model the entire dataset (Likelihood of data). Following Probability theory, the probability that ALL the observations are correct, is the multiplication of each single observation. Problem: if we multiply many numbers smaller than 1, we obtain a very little number, so we apply a logarythm to have a number that is a little more readable by a human. Finally, since optimization algorythms are made to minimize error functions, we add a negative sign in front of the formula:
\[ Log Loss = - \[ y \cdot \log{\hat{y}} + (1-y) \cdot \log(1-\hat{y}) \]\]



In this case, moments are simply the mean and the variance of gradients in time:

The first moment registers the average direction towards which a gradient is moving.
The second moment registers the “variance” of the gradients, which is how much the gradients change at each step.

These concepts come from linear algebra. It might be a little bit of an overkill to explain here, but in synthesis in linear algebra, when you want to decompose (find out its components) a complex vector, you project it onto a basis (i.e. usually the axes x, y, z, but you can take anything else as a reference). To understand the components of a vector, in linear algebra you do the Inner/Scalar product \(\langle U | V \rangle = \sum{U_i \cdot V_i}\) between the vector and the basis (ex: to find out the coordinate \(x\) of a vector \(v\) you do \(v_1x_1 + v_2x_2 + v_3x_3\), which will give you a single number).
In Machine Learning data is not certain, our observations follow a certain probability distribution. The moments are the projections (scalar products) of the probabilities distributions on your basis. If you project your observations \(x\) and their probabilities \(p\) on a linear basis (\(x^1\)) you obtain: \(\langle X | P \rangle = \sum{x_i \cdot p_i} = \mathbb{E}\[X\]\). This is both the first moment and the average. If, instead, you project your observations \(x\) and their probabilities \(p\) on a quadratic basis (\(x^2\)) you obtain the variance \(\mathbb{E}\[X^2\]\).

title: Rust Chapters 1-3
text:
To open the book even offline, run this command:
rustup doc --book
With Rust come some interesting tools:

Cargo: a dependency manager and build tool;
rustfmt formatting tool to have a consistent coding style;
The Rust Language Server powers IDE: inline error messages.




Rust Programming Language: Chapters 1 to 3

Table of Contents.
i. Chapter 1: Rust essentials and Cargo

Hello World

ii. Chapter 2
iii. Chapter 3: Common Programming Concepts

Variables
Constants and constant evaluation






Chapter 1 explains how to install Rust, how to write a “Hello, world!” program, and how to use Cargo, Rust’s package manager and build tool.

TOOL: rustup. The command-line tool for managing the version of Rust on your machine is rustup. You can access the documentation by running rustup doc.



To write the Hello World function we do like this:
fn main() {
    println!("Hello, world!");
}
The main() function is the first code that runs in every Rust program. Then we have to compile it. I had a problem with doing that, and I solved it by following a stackoverflow thread.
rustup toolchain install stable-x86_64-pc-windows-gnu
rustup default stable-x86_64-pc-windows-gnu
rustc main.rs
./main
Like in C++ we first need to compile the program (hence rustc main.rs): compiling means to generate a binary executable, which you can later execute. Interestingly enough, if you give somebody else the result file (main.exe) they don’t need to have Rust installed to be able to run it! An important part of this code is that println! calls a Rust macro. If it had called a function instead, it would be entered as println (without the !). Rust macros are a way to write code that generates code to extend Rust syntax, and it’s a topic from Chapter 20. Macros don’t always follow the same rules as functions. Additionally, like in C++, most lines of Rust code end with a semicolon (;).

TOOL: rustftm: To stick to a certain formatting standard, you can run rustfmt main.rs: it will rewrite the program with the correct spaces and all those practices to standardize code.


TOOL: cargo: Cargo is Rust’s build system and package manager.

If youy do:
cargo new hello_cargo
Cargo will create a new folder, complete with a .gitignore, a cargo.toml and a src directory: - The cargo.toml file is written in TOML (Tom’s Obvious, Minimal Language): the first line, [package], indicates that the following statements are configuring a package. Then the name, the version, and the edition of Rust to use. The last line, [dependencies], is the start of the project’s dependencies. In Rust, packages of code are referred to as crates. - In src/main.rs there is already an Hello World! Program (it is generated automatically). You can convert any project to the Cargo format by moving the code into a src directory and create a toml file by running cargo init.
With the following command we can create more files:
cargo build

an executable file in target/debug/hello_cargo.exe and not in the current directory (different from rustc main.rs which creates executables in the same directory as the source code);
a cargo.lock file that keeps track of dependencies (it updates automatically).

If you want to compile the code and run the executable all in one command, you can simply do cargo run, and it will not rebuild the executable file if the source code hasn’t changed, so it is pretty convenient! And if you just want to check if the code compiles and you don’t want to build an executable, you can do cargo check (faster than cargo build because it skips the building of an executable). Once ready to finalise the project, you can run cargo build --release. This can compile code with optimizations (although slow to compile), and the executable will be in target/release/hello_cargo.exe.

Chapter 2 is a hands-on introduction to writing a program in Rust, having you build up a number-guessing game. Here, we cover concepts at a high level, and later chapters will provide additional detail.



Although this chapter comes after 2, I decided to read it first because it will talk about concepts that are similar and different from Rust to other Programming languages.


Variables are immutable by default, although you can choose to make them mutable (not recommended). When a variable is immutable, its value cannot be changed: if you want a variable to be mutable you have to clearly state so.
fn main() {
  let mut x = 5;    // This will create a mutable variable
  let y = 6;      // This will create an immutable variable
}



Mostly used for values that are purposely hardcoded. They are also bound to a name but not allowed to change, but with a few differences: you cannot add mut, and you have to declare the type of the value. They can be declared in the global scope and they can be set as a constant expression but not as a result of a value that can only be computed at runtime (sometimes it is preferred to store values as an operation that an human can verify more easily and faster) but remember that only a set of all expressions can be evaluated at compile-time (“constant evaluation” is limited).

title: Welcome
text:
Collection of self-learning materials for Bioinformatics and Scientific Software development
This repository is dedicated to learning new skills through publicly available material. It is not only intended for me to organize my own self-learning but also to provide a collection of free, publicly available material online that can be useful to other early-career Bioinformatics Workflow scientists.

Programming languages

Rust | Book online and materials by Steve Klabnik, Carol Nichols, and Chris Krycho, with contributions from the Rust Community. Completed modules:

Chapter 1: Rust essentials and Cargo (rustup, rustftm, cargo);
Chapter 3 (on going): Common Programming Concepts (variables, constants and constant evaluation).

C++ | Course online by Codecademy. Completed modules:

Variables;
Conditionals & Logic;
Loops;
Vectors;
Functions (on going).




Collaborative programming

Version control with Git | Materials by SIB (Swiss Institute of Bioinformatics) funded by the Swiss State Secretariat for Education Research and Innovation (SERI) and the European Union’s Horizon Europe Framework Program (grant number 101080997). Completed modules:

Day 1: first steps with Git: fully completed. Topics: create and configure a Git repository, make commits, branching, remote collaboration, pull requests (GitHub);




Courses

title: Version control with Git
text:
This course covers Git’s usage through the command line (no Web version nor Visual Studio Code).


Lecturers: Robin Engler, Vassilios Ioannidis


The objectives of Git are:

having a distributed development (allow parallel, asynchronous work);
maintaining integrity and trust (identify changes in a repository);
enforcing documentation (each commit MUST have a message);
making it easy to branch and merge repositories (or line of development);
being free and open source.




The basic principle of Git is to take snapshots at user defined time points (not automatic). It keeps track of the order of snapshots and associates metadata to them: a snapshot with metadata is called a commit, and it has a unique ID, called a hash (40 characters long).

SHA-1 hash SHA-1 stands for Secure Hashing Algorithm 1. This algorithm is able to turn any binary input into a unique 40 character hexadecimal string.

Commits are stored in a repository: the actual Git repository is the folder called .git, which containts the repository history, metadata, configuration… but colloquially, the term repository refers to the entire directory under Git control. A working tree is the current content of a directory that is being tracked by Git: a branch is a line of development.

Local vs remote repository If you only create a Git repository on your computer, everything is local. If you want to collaborate with others, or have a remote backup, you need to create a remote repository on a server (e.g. GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket) and push your local repository to it. Backups are not automatically created.









Types of Git cases and their advantages






Single repo, single branch
Single repo, multiple branches
Multiple repos


Keep a documented log of your own work, so you can go back and compare earlier versions. Acts as a backup and you can distribute your code
Same advantages as single branch, but allows you to work on multiple features in parallel (i.e. published code and work in progress of new features).
Same advantages as the previous two, and allows to collaborate with others.




Size limits Git is not designed to handle large files, because for each edit the entire file needs to be stored (not only the edits!). If you want to version large files, you need to use Git LFS (Large File Storage): locally will create a reference to a large file, while the actual file will be saved in the object store. Not all hosting services support Git LFS. GitHub has a limit of 100 MB per file, and GitLab has a limit of 10 GB per repository. Additionally, for older commits, Git decreases disk space usage by storing only the differences between files, then compresses files in a single “pack file” (.pack extension) with an addociated index (.idx extension). This cannot be done for large files, which is why they are not supported by Git.



The minimum configuration is to set your name and email address, which will be associated with your commits. The global flag means that the configuration will be applied to all repositories on your computer. You can also set a default editor for Git commands that require one (e.g. commit messages).
git config --global user.name <user name>
git config --global user.email <email>

# Other configuration options:
git config --global core.editor <editor cmd. Ex: nano> 

# Access the config values:
git config --get user.name

# Show all configuration values:
git config --list --show-origin --show-scope

# Define a shortcut for a command:
git config --global alias.<new name/shortcut for a command> "command to associate with the shortcut"
A potential problem is the line-end character: Windows uses CRLF, while Linux and Mac use LF (\n). Git can automatically convert line endings to the correct format for the operating system. You can set this behavior with .
# Windows, convert LF to CRLF on checkout, and CRLF to LF on commit
git config core.autocrlf true 

# Linux/Mac, convert CRLF to LF on commit, but do not modify line endings on checkout
git config core.autocrlf input



You can either turn a local directory into a Git repo (git init, if you add –bare you do not create a working tree) or clone an existing repo (git clone https://github.com/….). To assess the current status of a repo:
git status     # Branch name, staged files (in green), unstaged files (red if they are modified), etc...
git log        # Commit history
git ls-files   # List files tracked by Git (you can have both tracked and untracked in the same repo)




Creating a commit is a 2-step process:

Stage the changes you want to include in the commit (add them to the Git index, also known as the staging area. It will create a copy in the .git folder) with git add.

Adding –edit or –patch allows you to select which changes to stage;
git add -u // –update stages all already tracked files but ignores the untracked ones;
If you change your mind, you can unstage changes with git rm –cached ;

Commit the staged changes with git commit -m “commit message…”;

You can stage and commit in one step with git commit –all -m “commit message…”, but it will only work for already tracked files.


A thing I (literally me, Flavia) have to work on is that not all current changes in the working tree need to be part of the next commit. I usually commit everything (with git add . if I didn’t delete anything, git add -A // –all if I did) to be able to work on the same thing from home and from University, but I should learn to commit only the changes that are related to a specific task. The course suggests that I should work on a temporary/feature branch and then later on merge it into the main one.

Files statuses - Tracked: file under version control, in the Git index, will be part of the next commit. - Unmodified: tracked, not changed since the last commit. - Modified: tracked files that have been changed. - Staged: in the Git index, will be part of the next commit. To remove them from the index, use git restore –staged < file > . To remove all files from the index at once, use git reset HEAD. Careful: you can remove files from the index using git rm –cached < file > but if you accidentally forget the flag, you will remove the file from the work tree as well; - If you do not add the –staged flag, it resets the file in the work tree to the version in the Git index. This is useful if you want to discard your own edits. If you want to retrieve the content of a file from an even earlier commit you can do git restore -s/–source < commit> < file > or git checkout < commit > < file >, but these commands will overwrite existing versions of the file in your working tree. Restore updates the file only in the working tree while checkout updates both the working tree and the index; - Unstaged: tracked, but not in the Git index, will not be part of the next commit. - To show the differences between two states of a git repo you can use: git diff <file>          git diff --cached          git diff --name-only # show only the file names, not changes.          git show # with no argument shows the latest commit on the current branch (HEAD) - Untracked: files in the folder but not under version control and not in the Git index, will not be part of the next commit. To stop them showing up in the git status output, you can add them to the .gitignore file (for files that should be ignored by every copy of the repository) or in the .git / info / exclude file (for files that should be ignored only in the local copy). - Ignored: not in the Git index, will not be part of the next commit, and will not be shown in git status.

To display the commit history, you can use:
git log
git log --oneline                           # compact view
git log --all --decorate --oneline --graph  # compact view of all the branches
Commits point to their direct parent, forming a DAG (Directed Acylic Graph) where no commit can be modified without altering all of its descendants.



Branching means to diverge from the main line of development:

they isolate new changes from stable code;
they isolate changes from different people;
on online repos, branches can be protected so only selected people can add commits to it.

To create and move between branches, you can use:
git branch < name >               # Create a new branch. Without name it lists local branches. Adding the flag -a it lists also the remote ones.
git switch < name >               # Switch to a branch
git switch -c < name >            # Create and switch to the new branch
git branch < name > < reference > # Creates a branch somewhere else than HEAD

The HEAD pointer: HEAD is a pointer to the latest commit on the current branch. New commits are added under the current HEAD. When you switch branch, HEAD moves too. You can also move HEAD to a specific commit, which is called a detached HEAD state (you are not on any branch). In this state, you can make changes and create commits, but they will be lost if you switch to another branch. To save them, you need to create a new branch and switch to it.

What happes when switching branches? The untracked files are unaffected by branch switches, while the rest of the content is updated to reflect the state of the commit of the active branch. If you have uncommitted changes the situation is a little bit more complicated: if changes do not conflict, then they are “carried over”, but if they do Git will stop the switching.



Merging (git merge < branch name >) means to incorporate changes from the specified branch into the currently active branch. There are two types of merging:

Fast-forward merge: this is possible if the branches have not diverged. If keeping an exact record of the history some people like to add a merge commit even if a fast-forward merge is possible, by adding –no-ff;
3-way merge: it creates an additional merge commit where conflicts may occur and need to be manually resolved. This preserves history perfectly but it can lead to messy histories. A merge can be aborted with  git merge –abort.
Branches can be moved/re-rooted on a different base commit by moving to the branch and then using git rebase < name of the branch to rebase on >. This command can generate conflicts which need to be resolved like during merges. This is kind of an additional type, which we can call rebase + fast forward merge: the history is cleaner but you also lose some branching history.

Choosing a type of merging comes from personal preference of readability and history-preservation trafeoff: honestly, they showed us an example of a messy history and I kinda prefer the cleaner look. Branches that are not used anymore can (and should) be deleted. To do so, first checkout of them and delete them:
git branch -d < branch >    # Safe option, only fully merged branches
git branch -D < branch >    # Not safe

Branch management strategies: you can decide to manage your project as you may see fit. The two most used strategies are:

GitFlow: the idea is to always have a dev branch on which new features are added until ready for a release;
Trunk-based development: there is not a dev branch but all features are merged directly to main when they are finished. Better when code is distributed via formal releases.


If you are not sure about merging a whole branch, you can cherry pick (git cherry-pick < commit >) which means to merge a single commit into the current branch, and not the whole branch itself. If, instead, you want to discard all edits you’ve done you can checkout an entire repo to an earlier commit (git checkout < commit >) which will restore the working tree, the index and will move the HEAD pointer to that commit. After the checkout you will enter a detached HEAD state, so you should go back to a regular branch.



A remote is a copy of Git repository that is stored on a server (GitHub or GitLab are common choices), which allows to backup the work, collaborate and distribute the work. A remote can be added using git remote add < remote name > < remote url > and the URL can be changed with git remote set-url.

HTTPS vs SSH: HTTPS and SSH are two different network protocols that machines use to communicate. If you clone via HTTPS you will need to provide a personal access token (PAT) as authentication credentials: if the repo is public the credentials are needed to push but not pull. If you clone via SSH you will need to add a public SSH key to the GitHub account. To create a PAT on Github, you go in your user profile, click on Settings and then Developer settings. There you will find Personal access tokens > Tokens (classic) > Generate new token (classic).

It is important, when working collaboratively, to check for edits on the branch by doing git fetch: if the history diverges, we can choose to either to git pull –no-rebase to merge them, or git pull –rebase.

Note: git pull is just a shortcut for git fetch followed by git merge –ff-only.

Earlier we talked about branches getting deleted if not in use anymore: when working remotely the deletion of a branch must be pushed! After doing git branch -d then you must run git push origin –delete. Other people having a local copy of the branch will not have it deleted with a normal git fetch: deleting while synchronicing is only possible by doing git fetch –prune.







Summary of commands (no commands)





Command
What it does


——–
——–


git clone
Create a local copy from an existing online repo


git remote add origin
Add a new remote to an existing local repo


git push
Push new commits on current branch to remote


git push -u origin
Additionally sets the upstream branch. Needed when pushing a branch for the first time, but not needed if the local branch was created from a remote branch


git push –force
Overwrites the branch on the remote with the local version (dangerous)


git fetch
Download all updates, even for non active branches


git pull
Download all updates and merge changes


git pull –no-rebase
Fetch + 3-way merge active branch


git pull –rebase
Fetch + rebase active branch


git pull –ff-only
Fetch + fast-forward merge


git remote -v
Display the remote(s) associated to a repo


git branch -vva
List branches of repo and their associated upstream (if any)



When working collaboratively you will have to get accostumed to Pull Request (GitHub)/ Merge Request (GitLab), which are a way to perform a merge operation on GitHub/GitLab instead of locally. This happens because remote, collaborative branches are usually protected and it gives the opportunity to repository owners to review changes before making them. To open a Pull request on GitHub:

First go on the project’s page on GitHub and go on the Pull requests tab;
Click on “New pull request” and select the branches to merge: if there are conflicts, you might need to rebase your branche and resolve them;
If everything is in order, click on “Create pull request” (optionally, enter a message for the peope that will review your pull request!).

I will not write here about GitLab because I personally like GitHub more.

title: Cheatsheet for Rust
Cheatsheet for Rust
text:
Initialize the package (new folder, with a .gitignore, a cargo.toml and a src directory with a .rs file): cargo new <project_name>
Create more files (an executable file in target/debug/.exe and not in the current directory, a cargo.lock for dependencies: cargo build
Convert any existing project to the cargo format: cargo init
Compile your code: rustc <project_name>.rs
Execute your code: ./<project_name>
Compile and exectute at the same time: cargo run
Check if code compiles without actually compiling: cargo check
Fix formatting to community standards: rustfmt <project_name>.rs

title: Lab 1: introduction to PyTorch
text:
Linear regression
Now that we have a GPU available, we are going to try out neural networks starting from a simple task: a linear regression.
As training set, we will generate a dataset from a linear function: the objective is, for our model, to estimate this function starting from the observed points.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

Xs = np.linspace(-20,20,100) # we start with a hundered X values between -20 and 20

Ys=Xs*5+3.5 # as our Xs are a numpy array, we can perform simple arithmetic on each element of Xs

#Now, we can plot the data we generated

plt.plot(Xs,Ys,"r.",label="training data")
plt.legend()








Now we will set up a very simple neural network with 1 input layer, 1 output layer and 4 hidden layers. Remember that the library PyTorch uses numpy arrays, so we have to define the type of data that goes in them (dtype), and then we need to reshape them into “torch vectors”. Other things we have to define, are: - the Loss Function (in this case MSE, but for a Logistic Regression, for example, we would use Log-Loss); - the optimizer (in this case SGD with a very small learning rate, but another popular choice is ADAm).

import torch.nn as nn

#we set the parameters of our simple network architecture
N_input=1
N_hidden=4
N_output=1

#create the model based on these parameters
model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(N_input, N_hidden),
    nn.Linear(N_hidden, N_output),
)

#convert our numpy arrays Xs and Ys into torch vectors we can use in training
inputs = torch.tensor(Xs.reshape((100,1)), dtype=torch.float32)
targets = torch.tensor(Ys.reshape((100,1)), dtype=torch.float32)

# We define the Loss function (Mean Square Error in this case, since this is a 
# linear regression task).
criterion =  torch.nn.MSELoss() 

# Construct the optimizer (Stochastic Gradient Descent in this case)
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.0001) 
# lr is the learning rate

We also set up a training loop. Remember: the number of epochs is, in simple terms, how many times we want the model to cycle through the neurons layers to try and converge to a model with the smallest Loss function possible.

N_epochs=3000
loss_vals=[]
# Gradient Descent
for epoch in range(N_epochs):
    # Forward pass: Compute predicted y by passing x to the model
    y_pred = model(inputs)

    # Compute and print loss
    loss = criterion(y_pred, targets)
    # Every 100 epochs, print the loss value, just to keep track
    if epoch % 100 == 0: 
        print('epoch: ', epoch, ' loss: ', loss.item())
        loss_vals.append(loss.item())

    # Zero gradients, perform a backward pass, and update the weights.
    optimizer.zero_grad()

    # perform a backward pass (backpropagation)
    loss.backward()

    # Update the parameters
    optimizer.step()

plt.plot(loss_vals,label="loss over epochs")
plt.legend()
